quranic_mention: Named across nine surahs — including 2:251, 17:55, 21:78-80, 27:15, 34:10-11 and 38:17-26
teaser: One clause of one ayah kills the giant. Then Allah hands him a throne, a scripture, and iron that softened in his hands — and tests him with two men and ninety-nine sheep.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: A youth in Talut's army who returned a king.
layers.source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir and Stories of the Prophets
layers.content:
Dawud, peace be upon him, arrives in the Qur'an inside somebody else's story. Surah al-Baqarah is describing Talut's outnumbered army facing Jalut, and then one clause turns the page of history: «وَقَتَلَ دَاوُودُ جَالُوتَ» — "and Dawud killed Jalut." (Quran 2:251)

That is the entire Qur'anic account of the killing. No sling, no stone, no exchange of words. Ibn Kathir does mention the sling, but he frames it exactly: Israelite accounts claimed that he killed Jalut with a slingshot. He passes it on as their claim and declines to raise its status. The detail everyone remembers is the one Allah did not record.

What Allah recorded is the sentence that follows. «وَآتَاهُ اللَّهُ الْمُلْكَ» — "and Allah gave him the kingdom"; «وَالْحِكْمَةَ» — "and wisdom"; «وَعَلَّمَهُ مِمَّا يَشَاءُ» — "and taught him of that which He willed." (Quran 2:251) Ibn Kathir reads the kingdom as Talut's kingdom passing into his hands, and the wisdom as what comes with prophethood.

So a young man of the Children of Israel who had no rank when the passage opened is holding, by the time it closes, both revelation and a throne. Almost no one in the Qur'an carries that pair. And the ayah will not let the reader admire him for it: it ends by stating that were it not for Allah checking one set of people by means of another, the earth would be filled with corruption (Quran 2:251). His rise is described as Allah's method of restraining ruin, not as Dawud's personal victory.

layers.title: The Voice
layers.subtitle: A scripture recited so beautifully that mountains answered back.
layers.source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir of Surah al-Isra, Surah Sad and Surah al-Anbiya
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah — the Scripture was made light upon Dawud; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
layers.content:
Dawud was given a book of his own. «وَآتَيْنَا دَاوُودَ زَبُورًا» — "and to Dawud We gave the Zabur." (Quran 17:55) Ibn Kathir treats the bare mention as a statement of his rank.

He was also given a voice to carry it. Al-Bukhari records from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: «خُفِّفَ عَلَى دَاوُدَ الْقُرْآنُ، فَكَانَ يَأْمُرُ بِدَوَابِّهِ فَتُسْرَجُ، فَكَانَ يَقْرَؤُهُ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَفْرُغَ» — the Scripture was made light upon Dawud, so he would order his mounts to be saddled and finish reciting it before the saddling was finished.

And creation joined the recitation. «إِنَّا سَخَّرْنَا الْجِبَالَ مَعَهُ يُسَبِّحْنَ بِالْعَشِيِّ وَالْإِشْرَاقِ» — "We made the mountains glorify Our praises with him in the late afternoon and at sunrise"; «وَالطَّيْرَ مَحْشُورَةً» — "and the birds, assembled"; «كُلٌّ لَهُ أَوَّابٌ» — "all of them obedient to him." (Quran 38:18-19) Ibn Kathir describes a bird that would hear the Zabur and refuse to fly on, hovering in the air to repeat after him, while the high mountains echoed his words back.

Generations later the standard had not moved. The Prophet ﷺ passed Abu Musa al-Ash'ari reciting at night, stopped to listen, and said: «لَقَدْ أُوتِيَ هَذَا مِزْمَارًا مِنْ مَزَامِيرِ آلِ دَاوُدَ» — this man has been given one of the melodies of the family of Dawud.

With the voice came authority: «وَشَدَدْنَا مُلْكَهُ وَآتَيْنَاهُ الْحِكْمَةَ وَفَصْلَ الْخِطَابِ» — "We made his kingdom strong and gave him wisdom and decisive speech." (Quran 38:20) Mujahid explained fasl al-khitab as soundness in speech and in judgement; Shurayh the judge and Qatadah read it as the settled procedure of testimony and oath. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the basis on which prophets ruled and on which this Ummah's courts still work.

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Two litigants, ninety-nine sheep, a verdict given too soon.
layers.source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir of Surah Sad
layers.content:
Two litigants climbed the wall into his mihrab, the private chamber where he had given orders that no one disturb him. «فَفَزِعَ مِنْهُمْ» — he was terrified of them (Quran 38:22). One said his brother had ninety-nine ewes while he had one, and was demanding that one as well: «وَعَزَّنِي فِي الْخِطَابِ» — "and he overpowered me in speech." (Quran 38:23)

Dawud ruled at once, for the man in front of him, without hearing the other side. Then the Qur'an turns: «وَظَنَّ دَاوُودُ أَنَّمَا فَتَنَّاهُ» — "and Dawud realised that We had tried him" — «وَخَرَّ رَاكِعًا وَأَنَابَ» — "and he fell down prostrate and turned in repentance" — «فَغَفَرْنَا لَهُ ذَٰلِكَ» — "so We forgave him that." (Quran 38:24-25)

Here the reader must be careful, and Ibn Kathir says so plainly. Around these ayat the exegetes assembled a long story, and he writes that it is mostly built on Isra'iliyyat narrations; that nothing has come from the infallible Prophet ﷺ about it that could be accepted as true; and that the one hadith reported by Ibn Abi Hatim has a chain that cannot be graded sahih, because it comes through Yazid ar-Raqashi, whose narrations the Imams treat as weak. His verdict is a rule for the reader: it is better to speak of this story briefly and refer knowledge of it to Allah, because the Qur'an is true and what it contains is true.

So the widely circulated account of Dawud and another man's wife is not part of this entry. Ibn Kathir did not certify it, and the ayat do not contain it. What the ayat contain is a prophet who judged before he listened, understood in an instant that he had been tested, went down in prostration, and was forgiven.

Ibn Kathir also notes that the prostration in Surah Sad is not one of the obligatory ones; it is a prostration of thanks, reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

layers.title: The Sign
layers.subtitle: Iron softened like thread, and armour still worn today.
layers.source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir of Surah al-Anbiya and Surah Saba
layers.content:
The signs given to Dawud were not spectacles staged for an audience. They were built into his work.

First, the mountains and the birds: «وَسَخَّرْنَا مَعَ دَاوُودَ الْجِبَالَ يُسَبِّحْنَ وَالطَّيْرَ» — "And We subjected the mountains and the birds to glorify Our praises along with Dawud." (Quran 21:79) Surah Saba puts it as a direct command to creation: «يَا جِبَالُ أَوِّبِي مَعَهُ وَالطَّيْرَ» — "O mountains, echo the praise with him, and you birds!" (Quran 34:10)

Then the metal. «وَأَلَنَّا لَهُ الْحَدِيدَ» — "And We made the iron soft for him." (Quran 34:10) Al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatadah and others explain that he needed neither furnace nor hammer; he could twist it in his hands like a thread. The purpose was immediately practical: «أَنِ اعْمَلْ سَابِغَاتٍ وَقَدِّرْ فِي السَّرْدِ» — "Make full coats of mail, and measure precisely the links." (Quran 34:11) Ibn Kathir explains the measurement as an engineer would: not so loose that the rings rattle, not so tight that the wearer cannot move.

And Surah al-Anbiya names the beneficiary. «وَعَلَّمْنَاهُ صَنْعَةَ لَبُوسٍ لَّكُمْ لِتُحْصِنَكُم مِّن بَأْسِكُمْ» — "And We taught him the making of armour for you, to protect you in your fighting." (Quran 21:80) Qatadah notes that before him they wore plate; Dawud was the first to link rings into mail. A miracle given to a prophet thousands of years ago is described as being for you.

The ayah ends with a question rather than applause: «فَهَلْ أَنتُمْ شَاكِرُونَ» — are you then grateful? And the response the Qur'an models is Dawud's own: «وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَضَّلَنَا عَلَىٰ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ» — "and they both said: all praise is for Allah, who has favoured us above many of His believing servants." (Quran 27:15)

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: His nightly rhythm is still the one recommended.
layers.source: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir of Surah Sad
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As — the most beloved prayer and fasting to Allah
layers.content:
After the forgiveness comes the appointment. «يَا دَاوُودُ إِنَّا جَعَلْنَاكَ خَلِيفَةً فِي الْأَرْضِ فَاحْكُمْ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ بِالْحَقِّ وَلَا تَتَّبِعِ الْهَوَىٰ فَيُضِلَّكَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ» — "O Dawud, We have made you a successor on the earth, so judge between people with truth, and do not follow desire, for it will lead you away from the path of Allah." (Quran 38:26) Al-Hasan al-Basri drew three duties for judges out of this and its parallels: do not sell your rulings, do not follow your own inclination, and do not fear anyone in what you judge.

Surah Sad opens his account by calling him possessed of strength and «أَوَّابٌ» — one who continually turns back to Allah (Quran 38:17). Qatadah said the strength was strength in worship, and the Two Sahihs preserve what that looked like. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: «أَحَبُّ الصَّلَاةِ إِلَى اللهِ صَلَاةُ دَاوُدَ، وَأَحَبُّ الصِّيَامِ إِلَى اللهِ صِيَامُ دَاوُدَ، كَانَ يَنَامُ نِصْفَ اللَّيْلِ، وَيَقُومُ ثُلُثَهُ، وَيَنَامُ سُدُسَهُ، وَكَانَ يَصُومُ يَوْمًا وَيُفْطِرُ يَوْمًا، وَلَا يَفِرُّ إِذَا لَاقَى» — the most beloved prayer to Allah is the prayer of Dawud, and the most beloved fasting to Allah is the fasting of Dawud: he slept half the night, stood a third of it, slept a sixth, fasted alternate days, and never fled when he met the enemy.

Read the arithmetic. He slept first, then rose, then slept again before dawn. He fasted every other day, not every day. When ibn 'Amr wanted to fast continuously, the Prophet ﷺ steered him to this instead. The most beloved worship to Allah, from the most powerful man of his age, was sustainable rather than extreme.

That is Dawud's inheritance: a king who worked iron with his own hands, a judge who was corrected and prostrated, and a schedule of worship so balanced that it is still the ceiling recommended to those who want more.

quiz.prompt: What does the Quran itself say about how Dawud killed Jalut?

options.text: That he struck him with a sling and a smooth stone
Only that Dawud killed Jalut — no weapon is named
That he defeated him in single combat with a sword
That an angel struck Jalut down

quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Kathir mentions the sling, but labels it: Israelite accounts claimed it. The most famous detail of the story is one Allah chose not to record.

quiz.prompt: According to Surah Saba, what was Dawud taught to make once iron was softened for him?

options.text: Ploughs and farming tools
The gates of Jerusalem
Coats of chain mail, with the links measured precisely
Musical instruments for the Zabur

quiz.citation: Quran 34:10-11 and Quran 21:80 — «أَنِ اعْمَلْ سَابِغَاتٍ وَقَدِّرْ فِي السَّرْدِ»
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Kathir explains the measurement with an artisan's precision: not so loose that the rings shake, not so tight that the wearer cannot move. Qatadah adds that Dawud was the first to link rings into mail.

quiz.prompt: In the case of the two litigants in Surah Sad, what was Dawud's actual mistake?

options.text: He took a bribe from the wealthier brother
He refused to hear the case at all
He ruled immediately without hearing the other party
He handed the case to Sulayman instead

quiz.scholar_reflection: The Quran records the swiftness of the ruling, the instant recognition that it was a test, the prostration, and the forgiveness. Nothing else in the passage is established.

quiz.prompt: How does Ibn Kathir handle the long story that commentators built around Quran 38:21-25?

options.text: He reports it as established fact from Sahih al-Bukhari
He says it rests mostly on Isra'iliyyat, that nothing sahih comes from the Prophet ﷺ about it, and that it is better to speak of it briefly and leave its knowledge to Allah
He says the ayat refer to a different prophet entirely
He grades the chain through Yazid ar-Raqashi as authentic

quiz.citation: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir of Surah Sad, on the story of the two litigants
quiz.scholar_reflection: He specifically names the weakness: the report of Ibn Abi Hatim comes through Yazid ar-Raqashi, whose narrations the Imams treat as weak. A famous story with no sound chain stays a story.

quiz.prompt: How did Dawud divide his night, according to the hadith in the Two Sahihs?

options.text: He stayed awake in prayer the entire night
He slept half of it, stood a third of it in prayer, then slept a sixth
He prayed only in the first third and slept the rest
He alternated, praying all night every second night

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As — «كَانَ يَنَامُ نِصْفَ اللَّيْلِ، وَيَقُومُ ثُلُثَهُ، وَيَنَامُ سُدُسَهُ»
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ gave this to a man who wanted to fast and pray without pause. Allah's most beloved schedule of worship includes deliberate sleep.

quiz.prompt: Dawud ruled for the man standing in front of him before the other side had spoken. Where does that happen to you?

options.text: In family disputes — I side with whoever tells me first
Online, where I decide who was wrong from one clip or screenshot
At work, where I back the person I already like
I do wait for both sides, but I have usually made up my mind by then

quiz.citation: Quran 38:23-24; cf. Quran 38:26 — «فَاحْكُمْ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ بِالْحَقِّ»
quiz.scholar_reflection: A prophet who had been given fasl al-khitab, decisive judgement, still needed this correction. Speed of verdict is not a sign of clarity; it is usually a sign of preference.
quiz.slider_label: How often do you judge before listening?

quiz.prompt: Iron softened in Dawud's hands so that he could make armour with them. What is the work your own hands actually do?

options.text: Something useful, though nobody would call it worship
Something that pays, and that I would drop tomorrow if it did not
Something I am good at but have never once thanked Allah for
Honestly, most of my day produces nothing I could point to

quiz.scholar_reflection: Allah made a king's craftsmanship a miracle and then said it was for you. The line between labour and worship is not the task; it is who you know gave you the hands.
quiz.slider_label: How much of your work do you connect to Allah?

quiz.prompt: The most beloved fasting and prayer to Allah were the sustainable kind, not the maximum. What is your instinct when you want to grow in worship?

options.text: Go as hard as possible and hope it holds
Add one thing and keep it small enough to survive a bad week
Wait for a season — Ramadan, a trip, a life change
I intend a lot and start almost nothing

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the prayer and fasting of Dawud; cf. Quran 38:17
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn 'Amr was praying all night and fasting all day, and was told to do less. Dawud's schedule was chosen by Allah as most beloved precisely because a body could carry it for a lifetime.
quiz.slider_label: How survivable is your current routine?

quiz.prompt: Ibn Kathir refused to certify the famous story about Dawud, even though everyone repeated it. How do you react when a scholar dismantles a story you grew up on?

options.text: Relieved — I would rather know than keep a good story
Resistant, because the story taught me something real
Confused about what is left to believe
I keep telling it anyway, because correcting people is awkward

quiz.citation: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir of Surah Sad; cf. Quran 17:36
quiz.scholar_reflection: The honour of a prophet is not defended by inventing a sin for him and then a repentance. Ibn Kathir's brevity here protects Dawud more than the long story ever did.
quiz.slider_label: How willing are you to drop a story you love?

quiz.prompt: Dawud was told: judge with truth, and do not follow desire. Which desire most often bends your decisions?

options.text: Wanting to be liked by the person in front of me
Wanting the outcome that costs me least
Wanting to be seen as fair, more than being fair
Wanting the argument to end, whatever the truth was

quiz.citation: Quran 38:26 — «وَلَا تَتَّبِعِ الْهَوَىٰ فَيُضِلَّكَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ»
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Hasan al-Basri read three duties into this: do not sell your judgement, do not follow your inclination, do not fear people. Naming your particular inclination is how you stop obeying it.
quiz.slider_label: Which way does your desire usually pull?
